name: Lisdexamfetamine (Vyvanse)

lead: Lisdexamfetamine (Vyvanse in the US, Elvanse in Europe) is a prescription stimulant approved for ADHD and for moderate to severe binge-eating disorder (BED) in adults. For looks, people interested in leaning out cite its appetite-reducing effect.

The drug is inactive until red blood cells release dextroamphetamine, which raises norepinephrine and dopamine signalling and reduces appetite. Trials in BED measured binge-eating days, not body weight as a cosmetic goal, and the US label states it is not indicated for weight loss.

paras: It is prescribed as a once-daily capsule or chewable tablet. Its gradual release makes it a smoother option than immediate-release amphetamine for some people. Appetite effects appear soon after starting.

It is a Schedule II controlled substance in the US with a boxed warning for abuse, misuse and addiction. The label also warns of cardiovascular risks, raised blood pressure and heart rate, and psychiatric reactions such as mania or psychosis, and it is contraindicated with MAO inhibitors. It requires a prescription.

social.title: FDA approves multiple generics of ADHD and BED treatment Vyvanse

angle.text: Vyvanse is discussed for its appetite-reducing effect: eating less leads to weight loss and a leaner look. It is approved for ADHD and binge-eating disorder; weight loss for appearance has not been the studied purpose.

lead: Lisdexamfetamine dimesylate, marketed as Vyvanse in the United States and Elvanse in Europe, is a central nervous system stimulant and a prodrug of dextroamphetamine. It is formed by attaching the amino acid lysine to dextroamphetamine, and the active drug is released after enzymatic hydrolysis in the bloodstream.[1][2][3] It is prescribed for attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) in children aged 6 and older and adults, and for moderate to severe binge-eating disorder (BED) in adults.[2]

Its link to appearance runs through appetite and body weight. Decreased appetite and weight loss are among the common effects of amphetamines, and in the pivotal BED trial the treated groups lost several kilograms on average over the study period while the placebo group did not.[4][3] People who discuss it in appearance communities describe the chain as stimulant, then reduced hunger, then lower intake and a leaner look; on looksmax.org one poster asked about experiences with hunger suppression, longevity and strength.[5] The US label does not list weight loss as an indication and carries a boxed warning for abuse, misuse and addiction.[2]

Research on the drug consists of randomised trials in ADHD and BED, systematic reviews and network meta-analyses, and prescribing information. A 2018 network meta-analysis of 133 randomised trials in The Lancet Psychiatry placed amphetamines, the class that includes lisdexamfetamine, as the most effective short-term option for adults with ADHD in clinician ratings.[6] No published trial has tested it for cosmetic goals in people without ADHD or BED.[2][4]
infobox: Robert Oberlender, New River Pharmaceuticals (as NRP104); later Shire, then Takeda[3]
Prescription only; Schedule II (US), Class B (UK), Schedule 8 (Australia)[3]

paras: The US label lists two indications: ADHD in patients aged 6 years and older, and moderate to severe binge-eating disorder in adults.[2] The FDA first approved it in February 2007 for children with ADHD and extended the approval to adults in 2008, and approved it for BED in January 2015; Health Canada approved it in 2009 and the EU in 2012.[1][3] As of July 2024 it was the only FDA-approved drug for BED, according to Wikipedia.[3][7]

In a four-week trial of 420 adults with ADHD, all three tested dose groups improved more than placebo on the ADHD Rating Scale, with changes of about 16 to 19 points against about 8 for placebo, and 57 to 62% of treated participants were rated much or very much improved against 29% on placebo.[8] Phase III pediatric trials in children aged 6 to 12 reported similar findings for ADHD symptom scores.[9][10] Narcolepsy is an off-label use.[3]

Amphetamines suppress appetite, and decreased appetite and weight loss are recognised effects of the class; among common adverse effects in trials, Wikipedia lists decreased appetite, insomnia, dry mouth and weight loss.[3] The BED indication is a psychiatric one, and the US label says lisdexamfetamine is not indicated for weight loss.[2] Binge-eating disorder is associated with overweight, obesity and metabolic comorbidities, and up to 70% of people with BED may have obesity according to one estimate summarised on Wikipedia.[11][7]

Wikipedia's article on the drug argues that improved cognitive control, not appetite suppression, is the main therapeutic effect in BED, noting that anti-obesity drugs did not significantly reduce binge symptom severity despite causing weight loss.[3] No published trial has tested lisdexamfetamine for cosmetic weight loss or other appearance goals in people without BED or ADHD.[2]

Lisdexamfetamine is pharmacologically inactive until it is converted to dextroamphetamine, a step carried out by enzymes in red blood cells with a half-life of about one hour.[1][3] Amphetamines are sympathomimetic amines that raise extracellular norepinephrine and dopamine.[12] The US label states that the exact mode of therapeutic action in ADHD and BED is not known.[2]

Dextroamphetamine levels peak around 3.5 hours after a dose in children and about 5 hours in adults, with effects lasting roughly 12 to 14 hours according to Grokipedia; Wikipedia gives onset within 90 minutes and duration up to 14 hours.[1][3] The prodrug design is intended to give a longer effect and lower misuse potential, and human abuse-liability studies reported lower drug-liking scores than immediate-release dextroamphetamine at approved doses, though abuse potential rises substantially when doses are greatly exceeded.[1][3] The US label nonetheless warns that misuse, including by non-oral routes, can cause overdose and death.[2]

Wikipedia credits Robert Oberlender of New River Pharmaceuticals with developing the compound as NRP104; Shire acquired New River and Takeda later acquired Shire.[3] The US patent expired on 24 February 2023, after the FDA had given tentative approval to generic formulations in 2015, and multiple generics were approved in 2023, an event that drew discussion on Hacker News.[3][13]

Prescribing is large: in 2023 it was the 76th most commonly prescribed medicine in the United States, with more than 9 million prescriptions, and US production quotas for 2016 were 29,750 kg.[3] Binge-eating disorder itself was first described in 1959 as night-eating syndrome by Albert Stunkard, appeared in the DSM in 1994 as a proposed condition, and became a formal diagnosis in DSM-5 in 2013.[7]

The boxed warning states that lisdexamfetamine has a high potential for abuse and misuse that can lead to a substance use disorder, including addiction, and that misuse of CNS stimulants can result in overdose and death.[2]

Warnings and precautions in the label include risks in patients with serious cardiac disease, increased blood pressure and heart rate, and psychiatric adverse reactions. Prescribers are advised to screen for risk factors for mania and to consider stopping the drug if new psychotic or manic symptoms appear.[2] Use with monoamine oxidase inhibitors can cause hypertensive crisis and is contraindicated.[2] Wikipedia lists rare serious effects including mania, sudden cardiac death in people with underlying heart problems, stimulant psychosis and serotonin syndrome, and notes that Australian labelling contraindicates use in anorexia.[3] Grokipedia also lists growth suppression in children among the monitored effects.[1]

On pregnancy, the label states that available human data are insufficient to establish a drug-associated risk of birth defects or miscarriage, while noting that adverse outcomes such as premature delivery and low birth weight have been seen in infants of mothers dependent on amphetamines.[2]

Lisdexamfetamine is a Schedule II controlled substance in the United States and requires a prescription.[1][2] Wikipedia lists it as Class B in the UK and New Zealand, Schedule 8 in Australia, Schedule I under Canada's CDSA, and prescription-only in the EU.[3] Generic versions are available, and bioequivalence trials of generic capsules against the branded product (marketed as Elvanse in Europe) have been registered.[14]

On looksmax.org the drug is discussed mainly as an appetite suppressant and performance aid; one thread asked for personal experiences with Vyvanse or other stimulants, naming hunger suppression, longevity and strength as the effects of interest, and replies from other members called stimulants risky.[5] Looksmaxxing forums also host threads about obtaining ADHD medication without a prescription, which are not summarised here; the label and regulators describe it as a prescription-only controlled drug.[2][3]

A randomized, placebo-controlled trial in adults with moderate to severe BED, published in JAMA Psychiatry in 2015 (30 sites, 11 weeks, 255 participants analysed), tested three fixed dose arms against placebo: the two higher arms reduced binge-eating days significantly while the lowest did not.[4][4] Binge-eating cessation for four weeks was reached by 21.3% on placebo versus 42.2% and 50.0% in the two higher arms; mean weight change was about -0.1 kg on placebo and -3.1 to -4.9 kg across treated arms.[4] Any treatment-emergent adverse event occurred in 58.7% of placebo participants and 84.7% of treated participants.[4]

A 2019 meta-analysis of 81 randomised trials (7,515 people) found large effects of psychotherapy, mainly cognitive behavioural therapy, on binge episodes against wait-list, and small effects of drug treatments against pill placebo, with lisdexamfetamine consistent with that pattern.[15] A 2022 meta-review of eating disorder treatment meta-analyses also covered this evidence base.[16]

A 2018 network meta-analysis in The Lancet Psychiatry of 133 double-blind randomised trials found amphetamines the most efficacious class in adults (standardised mean difference about -0.79 against placebo in clinician ratings) and in children in clinician ratings (about -1.02), while dropout from adverse effects was higher on amphetamines than placebo; the authors favoured amphetamines for adults and methylphenidate for children as first-choice short-term treatments.[6] Registered pediatric and adult trials include a phase III study in 297 children aged 6 to 12 and the 2008 placebo-controlled adult study described above.[8][10]

Smaller trials have examined lisdexamfetamine in bulimia nervosa (a terminated phase 2 study),[17] cocaine dependence (a terminated pilot),[18] and residual symptoms and cognitive impairment in major depressive disorder.[19] A phase 4 study examined its cardiovascular effects in adults with ADHD, including hypertensive participants,[20] and another looked at its pharmacokinetics after bariatric surgery.[21] These are not approved uses.

lore.intro: On looksmax.org lisdexamfetamine appears in a small number of threads, mostly as an appetite-suppressing stimulant or a way to train and focus, with other members warning about dopamine-related risks.[5]
